## Executive Summary

Current evidence from 2025–2026 indicates that generative AI coding assistants have become a standard component of software engineering workflows, with over 75% of developers reporting daily usage [S4]. Empirical studies, including randomized controlled trials and large-scale field experiments, consistently demonstrate significant productivity gains, with one major study reporting a 26.08% increase in completed tasks [S1]. While developer satisfaction remains high, with enterprise trials reporting 72% satisfaction rates [S2], the magnitude of objective productivity improvements varies by task type and developer experience level. The evidence suggests that AI assistants are most effective for routine, well-scoped tasks, offering up to 55% faster completion times in specific contexts [S4, S2].

## Empirical Evidence of Productivity Gains

The most robust evidence for productivity improvements comes from controlled experiments and field studies. A prominent randomized controlled trial found that developers using AI coding assistants completed tasks 26.08% faster than those in the control group [S1]. This finding is supported by enterprise deployments and controlled studies, which indicate that AI tools can accelerate task completion by up to 55% for well-scoped tasks [S4, S2]. These gains are not uniform across all scenarios; productivity improvements are often more pronounced for less experienced developers or in specific task categories such as code generation and unit testing [S1, S2]. This suggests that the technology acts as a force multiplier for routine coding activities, reducing the cognitive load associated with boilerplate code and standard implementations.

## Developer Adoption and Perceived Utility

Adoption of AI coding assistants has reached a saturation point in the industry, with surveys indicating that over 75% of developers now use these tools daily [S4]. This widespread integration is reflected in high satisfaction rates; specific enterprise trials have reported 72% satisfaction among users [S2]. There is a strong consensus between subjective perception and objective usage, as surveys and RCTs consistently show that developers perceive productivity gains even when objective metrics vary slightly across different study designs [S2]. The high level of daily use suggests that AI assistants have moved beyond experimental tools to become essential infrastructure for modern software development teams, fundamentally altering how code is written, reviewed, and maintained.

*Citations: [S2], [S4]*

## Consistency and Contextual Nuances in the Evidence

While the direction of the impact is consistent across sources, the magnitude of productivity gains depends heavily on context. The evidence agrees that AI coding assistants generally improve task completion rates and time-to-completion, particularly for routine or well-defined tasks [S1, S2, S4]. However, the benefits are not universal; they are more significant for junior developers or in tasks with clear, repetitive patterns [S1, S2]. No severe conflicts were detected in the analyzed evidence, indicating a stable consensus that AI assistants provide a net positive impact on productivity. The variation in reported metrics (ranging from 26% to 55% improvements) likely reflects differences in task complexity, developer experience levels, and the specific AI models used in each study [S1, S4].
